about.title: Linear and Nonlinear Functions
about.length_note: About 30 minutes fits. There are four small ideas: constant rate of change, straight-line graphs, y = mx + b, and nonlinear examples. Each gets a worked example and a check, then there is a short practice set. The practice can be paused and picked up later.

sources.title: Section 4.4 Comparing Linear and Nonlinear Functions (Grade 8, Chapter 4 Functions)
4.8.4 Rate of Change of Linear Functions - Algebra 1
Illustrative Mathematics Grade 8, Unit 5, Lesson 8: Linear Functions (teacher notes)
8th Grade Functions, Lesson 8: Are You Sure?

say.text: Welcome back. Today we learn to tell straight-line functions from ones that bend. Take your time, and pause whenever you like.
First, a reminder from last class. A function is a rule that gives each input exactly one output.

show.text: function: each input gets exactly one output

ask.q: In a function, how many outputs does each input get?
wrong: Two
As many as you like
None
ask.why: A function is a rule that gives each input exactly one output. That is what makes it a rule you can rely on.

say.text: Now a new idea: rate of change. It tells how much the output changes when the input changes. You divide the change in y by the change in x.

show.text: x: 0, 1, 2, 3  |  y: 5, 8, 11, 14  |  y goes up 3 each time x goes up 1, so the rate of change is 3

ask.q: Here is a table. x: 1, 2, 3. y: 4, 7, 10. What is the rate of change?
ask.why: y goes from 4 to 7, which is up 3. Then it goes from 7 to 10, which is up 3 again. x goes up 1 each time, so the rate of change is 3 divided by 1, which is 3.

say.text: A linear function has a constant rate of change. Constant means the same everywhere. You can pick any two points and get the same answer.

show.text: x: 3, 6, 9, 12  |  y: 40, 32, 24, 16  |  every time x goes up 3, y goes down 8. The rate is constant, so it is linear.

ask.q: Is this table linear? x: 0, 2, 4, 6. y: 1, 5, 9, 13.
ask.right: Yes. y goes up 4 every time x goes up 2.
wrong: No, because y changes every time.
No, because x does not go up by 1.
There is not enough information to tell.
ask.why: Every step has the same pattern: x up 2 and y up 4. The rate of change is the same each time, so the function is linear. y is allowed to change, and x does not have to go up by 1. What matters is that the rate stays the same.

say.text: One careful point. If the x steps are not equal, divide each y change by its x change. The answers should match.

show.text: x: 1, 2, 4  |  y: 3, 6, 12  |  3 ÷ 1 = 3 and 6 ÷ 2 = 3. The rate is 3 both times, so it is linear.

ask.q: Is this table linear? x: 0, 1, 3. y: 2, 4, 8.
ask.right: Yes. The rate is 2 both times.
wrong: No, because y goes up by 2 and then by 4.
No, because the x steps are different.
Not enough information.
ask.why: From x = 0 to 1, y goes up 2, so the rate is 2 divided by 1, which is 2. From x = 1 to 3, y goes up 4 while x goes up 2, so the rate is 4 divided by 2, which is also 2. The rates match, so it is linear.

say.text: If the rate of change is not constant, the function is nonlinear. Look at the table and compare the jumps.

show.text: x: 0, 1, 2, 3  |  y: 2, 4, 8, 16  |  y jumps by 2, then 4, then 8. The rate keeps changing, so it is nonlinear.

ask.right: Nonlinear. The jumps are 2, then 3, then 4.
wrong: Linear, because y always goes up.
Linear, because the numbers get bigger in order.
Linear, because x goes up by 1 each time.
ask.why: x goes up by 1 each time, but y jumps by 2, then 3, then 4. The rate of change is not constant. Going up is not the test. The test is going up by the same amount.

say.text: Now graphs. A constant rate means the same steepness everywhere. So the graph of a linear function is a straight line.

ask.q: A function's graph is a straight line. What does that tell you about its rate of change?
wrong: It keeps getting bigger.
It keeps getting smaller.
It is always zero.
ask.why: A straight line has the same steepness everywhere. Same steepness means the same rate of change. The rate does not have to be zero. A line can slope up or down.

say.text: A nonlinear function has a graph that is not a straight line. It bends, because the rate keeps changing.
Here is the classic nonlinear example: the area of a square. If the side is s, the area is A = s times s, written s². A side of 3 uses 9 blocks.

ask.q: Using A = s², what is the area of a square with side 2?
ask.why: s² means s times s. So 2 times 2 is 4. The answers 6 and 8 come from adding or doubling by mistake.

say.text: Let's test it. Sides 1, 2 and 3 give areas 1, 4 and 9. The area goes up by 3, then by 5. The rate is not constant.

show.text: A = s²: the points (1,1), (2,4), (3,9) are not on a straight line

ask.q: Is the area function A = s² linear?
ask.right: No. Its rate of change is not constant, and its graph bends.
wrong: Yes, because the area always gets bigger.
Yes, because it has just one letter, s.
There is no way to tell.
ask.why: The points (1,1), (2,4) and (3,9) do not lie on one straight line. The area grows by 3 and then by 5, so the rate is not constant. That makes it nonlinear.

say.text: Now equations. If a function can be written as y = mx + b, it is linear, and its graph is a straight line.
Here is what the letters mean. m is the rate of change, which is also the slope. b is where the line crosses the y-axis. In y = 3x + 2, start at 2 and go up 3 for each step in x.

show.text: m = rate of change (slope)  |  b = where the line crosses the y-axis  |  y = 3x + 2 has m = 3 and b = 2

ask.q: In y = 5x - 4, what is the rate of change?
ask.why: In y = mx + b, the rate of change is m, the number multiplied by x. Here m is 5. The -4 is b, where the line crosses the y-axis.

say.text: The sign of m tells you the direction. A positive m means y goes up as x goes up. A negative m means y goes down. If m is 0, the line is flat.

show.text: m positive: rising  |  m negative: falling (like the table where y dropped by 8)  |  m = 0: flat

ask.q: Is the line y = -2x + 7 rising or falling?
wrong: Rising
Flat
It is not a line.
ask.why: m is -2, which is negative, so y goes down as x goes up. The equation still has the form y = mx + b, so it is a line.

say.text: For nonlinear equations, a good clue is that x gets squared, as in s². Those do not fit y = mx + b. Sometimes an equation needs tidying first. For example, 2x + y = 9 becomes y = -2x + 9.

wrong: y = x²
y = x² + 2
y = 2x²
ask.why: y = 6x + 1 has the form y = mx + b, with m = 6 and b = 1. The other three have x squared, so they are not in that form. Their graphs are not straight lines.

say.text: So you have three ways to check. In a table, look for the same change in y for the same change in x. In a graph, look for a straight line. In an equation, look for y = mx + b.

show.text: Table: constant rate  |  Graph: straight line  |  Equation: y = mx + b

say.text: Time to practise. Take it slowly. Each question uses a tool we just learned.
A gym charges $20 to join, plus $10 each month. The cost is C = 10m + 20, where m is the number of months.

ask.q: Is the gym cost function linear or nonlinear?
ask.right: Linear. It has the form y = mx + b with m = 10 and b = 20.
wrong: Nonlinear, because the cost keeps growing.
Nonlinear, because there are two numbers.
Not enough information.
ask.why: The equation fits y = mx + b. The cost goes up $10 every month, so the rate of change is constant. The $20 joining fee is b, the starting amount.

say.text: Now compare two squares. Perimeter is P = 4s. Area is A = s². Both start at side 1 and grow.

ask.q: Which one is linear: the perimeter P = 4s or the area A = s²?
wrong: The area, A = s²
Both are linear.
Neither is linear.
ask.why: P goes up by 4 every time s goes up by 1, so its rate is constant. It also fits y = mx + b, with m = 4 and b = 0. A goes up by 3, then 5, so it is not constant. Area is the nonlinear one.

say.text: One more table. This one is going down.

ask.q: Is this table linear? If it is, what is the rate of change?
ask.right: Linear, with a rate of change of -3.
wrong: Linear, with a rate of change of 3.
Nonlinear, because y is going down.
Nonlinear, because the numbers are not the same.
ask.why: y drops by 3 every time x goes up by 1, so the rate is constant. Since y goes down, the rate is negative: -3. A function can go down and still be linear.

say.text: Last one, a tricky one. A flat line has m = 0. Its y never changes.

ask.q: Is a flat, horizontal line a linear function?
ask.right: Yes. It has the form y = mx + b with m = 0.
wrong: No, because y never changes.
No, because it has no slope.
No, because it is not going up or down.
ask.why: A flat line has a constant rate of change, and that rate is 0. It fits y = mx + b with m = 0, so it is linear. Its graph is a straight line.

say.text: Well done. To finish, here are the big ideas.

show.text: Linear: constant rate of change, straight-line graph, y = mx + b  |  Nonlinear: the rate changes and the graph bends, like A = s²  |  Next class: using linear functions to model real life
